REJB 2001-24813 - Texte
intégral

CITATION: Rosenberg c. Outremont
(City)

Cour
supérieure

CANADA

PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC

DISTRICT DE Montréal

NO : 500-05-060659-008

DATE :  2001-06-21

EN PRÉSENCE DE :

Allan R. Hilton
, J.C.S.

Michael Rosenberg, Jack Hartstein, Jonathan Fisher, Alex Werzberger et Eliezer
Frankforter

Petitioners

v.

City of Outremont

Respondent

et

Mouvement laïque québécois

Intervenant

Hilton J.C.S.:-

I Introduction and Nature of the Proceedings

1
Legal proceedings that
assert claims based on freedom of religion are bound to excite passion. This is
one such case.

2
The Petitioners Michael
Rosenberg, Jack Hartstein, Jonathan Fisher, Alex Werzberger and Eiliezer
Frankforter are all practising members of the Orthodox Jewish faith who reside
in the Respondent City of Outremont. They have presented a motion for
declaratory judgment in which they seek to have it declared that they are
entitled to erect and maintain a structure known as an
eruv
1

on private property in Outremont that traverses over part of the public domain
in that municipality, namely, City streets.

3
The conclusions of their
motion, as re-amended during the hearing, ask the Court to issue the following
declarations:

1.

a) That Petitioners, and others
of similar beliefs are entitled to put up an
Eruv
(described in next
paragraph) linking areas and attached to private properties with the consent of
owners;

b) The
Eruv
is to be
installed at the upper level of said building, approximately fifteen feet above
ground, and consists of a string or other object of similar radius along with
associated rods;

c) Persons putting up new
Eruvs

or moving existing
Eruvs
, will notify the City of Outremont of the
locations of said
Eruvs
;

d) The
Eruvs
will be
installed within the zone circumscribed in the attached map;

e) No more than two
Eruvs

per City block will be required inside the zone;

2. ...

3. That the City has no right to
pull down such an
Eruv
;

4. That there is no by-law or law
restricting the erection of such a “structure” or alternatively
that Petitioners are entitled to accommodation under the
Quebec Charter
of Human Rights and Freedoms
and the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
.

4
The Petitioners also
claim to be entitled to have provisional execution ordered notwithstanding
appeal in the event their proceedings are successful.

5
The zone “on the
attached map” that is referred to in paragraph 1(d) of the conclusions
extends over several City blocks. It is the area in Outremont where the Court
was told that the Petitioners and many other Orthodox Jews live who might wish
to benefit from having
eruvin
. The zone is bounded to the west by Stuart
Avenue, to the north by Van Horne Avenue, to the east by Hutchison Avenue, to
the south by St. Joseph Boulevard, and to the south-east by Côte St.
Catherine Road.

II The Facts and the Contentions of the Parties

6
The precise nature of an
eruv

is described in many ways in the affidavit material and exhibits, as well as in
a judgment of the Supreme Court of New York in Queens County to which reference
will be made later in these reasons.

7
Essentially, an
eruv

is a notional concept by which an otherwise open area is closed by the
attachment of barely visible wires or strings to freestanding structures. The
purpose of an
eruv
is to avoid the prohibition in Jewish Law of removing
things from one domain to another on the Sabbath and on Holidays. From a
practical point of view, without an
eruv
, an Orthodox Jew is effectively
housebound on the Sabbath and religious holidays if he or she wishes to or is
required to take anything out of the house and bring it on to other property. This
prevents, for example, such commonplace activity as pushing a stroller with
young children, carrying medication, or bringing food to a neighbour's home.

8
The rationale for and
purpose of an
eruv
is described in the following manner in an exhibit
attached to the affidavit of Rabbi David Merling that discusses
eruvin

in the Boston area:

The Sabbath of the Jew is a very
special time of the week. From Friday evening just prior to sunset until
Saturday evening when the stars begin to appear, a spirit of calm and
restfulness descends which contrasts with the fast pace of daily weekday life. For
the traditional Jew, the Sabbath, like all other aspects of life, is defined by
a complete set of legal guidelines which describe the “do's” and
“don't's” of the day. Among the restrictions accepted by
traditional Jews are the prohibitions of carrying objects from public domains
to private domains and vice versa, and the carrying within a public domain. By
public domains are meant non-residential areas including streets,
thoroughfares, plazas (“open areas”), highways, etc. By private domains
are meant residential areas such as homes and apartments, i.e. enclosed areas,
and areas which are surrounded by a “wall” and can be deemed to be
“closed off” from the surrounding public domains. Within the latter
areas, one is permitted to carry....

The purpose of an
Eruv
is
to integrate (the Hebrew word “
eruv
” to mix or join
together) a number of private and public properties into one larger private
domain. Consequently, individuals within the
Eruv
district are then
permitted to move objects across, what was before the erection of the
Eruv
,
a public domain-private domain boundary. Thus, one may then carry from ones'
home to the sidewalk and then, for example, to someone else's home.

9
The community impact of
having an
eruv
is described in the same exhibit as follows:

The question may be raised: what
tangible changes occur as a result of having an
Eruv
in Boston? As
mentioned above, traditional Jews are prevented, in the absence of an
Eruv
,
from carrying anything outside of one's home during the Sabbath. This
restriction is extremely hard on Jewish community and family life, since, for
example, families with very young children who are not yet able to walk are
“house-bound” unable to get either to synagogue or to friends'
homes. An
Eruv
permits the use of strollers and walkers. It permits
parents of young children to reach a synagogue on the Sabbath, to meet with
friends at neighborhood homes, and to share a festive Sabbath meal together. Another
population benefitting from the
Eruv
district is the elderly whose use
of canes, wheelchairs, and other ancillary items is now possible. The
Eruv

facilitates greater involvement of the disabled population, in general, into
the community on the Sabbath. Further, and very importantly, it will encourage
greater interaction among the members of the larger Jewish community (notably
by allowing more inter-family contact and at greater distances than are
presently possible).

10
The uncontested evidence
is to the effect that
eruvin
are found in many Canadian cities,
including Montreal and several of its suburbs such as Town of Mount Royal,
Ville St. Laurent, Dollard-des-Ormeaux and Côte St. Luc. The evidence
also shows that they are widespread in communities of varying sizes in several
states of the United States such as New York, Connecticut, Florida, California,
Massachusetts, Missouri, and New Jersey, as well as in major cities in other
countries around the world such as France, Australia, and Germany.

11
The City of Outremont
objects to the alignment of such barely visible wires from house to house to
the extent that the wires cross City streets, even when the owners of the
houses in question consent to their attachment. The City has not enacted any
formal prohibition, but it is not disputed that when it becomes aware of the
placement of an
eruv
, its employees are dispatched to dismantle it.

12
The Court does not know
with certainty to what extent or with what frequency
eruvin
have been
erected in Outremont over the years. Nevertheless, it does not appear to have
been only a recent phenomenon. What is clear, however, is that the City began
to dismantle them not long ago in response to complaints from some of its
residents. Attempts by interested persons to persuade the City to abandon this
practice have met with failure. According to Mr. Rosenberg's supporting
affidavit, the Mayor said at a City Council meeting on October 25, 2000 that in
his view the City “did not have jurisdiction” to permit anything to
be done on religious grounds because of its secular vocation. This view is
reflected in paragraphs 6 and 14 to 17 inclusively of the City's written
Contestation in which the same essential position is put forth.

13
The City even carried
out the dismantling of
eruvin
on the eve of the Jewish High Holiday of
Rosh
Hashana
last year. At the same time, the City's employees, with an excess
of enthusiasm for the task, dismantled an
eruv
that had been legally
erected in the City of Montreal pursuant to a resolution of its Executive
Committee dating back to 1989.

14
At the hearing, the City
argued that its position does not constitute an interference with the freedom
of religion of the Petitioners, since the restriction they seek to alleviate by
the erection of
eruvin
is imposed by Jewish Law and not by Outremont. It
further argues that the place in which freedom of religion may be exercised is
not a component part of the guarantee such that it can legally control the use
of the air over its streets without violating the Petitioners' freedom of
religion. It also contends that to the extent the Court finds that the conduct
of the municipality violates freedom of religion, such conduct is justifiable
in light of its duty to maintain the public domain accessible to all residents
of Outremont on the same basis and without distinction. Finally, the City
considers the re-amended conclusions of the motion to be impermissibly vague
and incapable of enforcement if granted.

15
The position of the City
is supported by the
Mouvement Laïque Québécois
. It
has intervened with the consent of the Petitioners, and has attached affidavits
from four Outremont residents: Céline Forget, who is a municipal
councillor, Marie FitzGerald, Michel Vais and Danielle Rossignol. Three of the
affiants live within the perimeter in which the Petitioners claim relief.

16
The Intervenant argues
preliminarily that the Petitioners' proceedings are defective in that all of
the persons potentially affected by the granting of the relief claimed, namely
the residents within the area described in paragraph [5] above, have not been
served with the proceedings. Thus, it contends that these Outremont residents
have been deprived of an opportunity to be heard.

17
To the extent that the
contention is a valid one, it has surely been palliated by the adept arguments
of counsel for the City of Outremont and by the equally capable presentation of
arguments on behalf of the Intervenant. The Court will therefore consider it no
further.

18
It is also suggested
that the erection of
eruvin
involuntarily place non-members of the
Orthodox Jewish faith within what amounts to a religious enclave with which
they do not wish to be associated. A judgment maintaining the relief being
sought would inevitably create what amounts to an officially recognized
religious territory, they say. Such a territory would not be at all similar to
having religious institutions such as churches or synagogues in the City, since
they are free to go in or not to go into a church or a synagogue. In effect,
they complain that they could never avoid the effect of the
eruvin
since
their presence would be permanent, and that they could go nowhere outside their
residences without having to confront the fact that they live within an
eruv
.

19
While all the while
recognizing freedom of religion for the Petitioners and anyone else, the
Intervenant and its supporters claim the right of freedom
from
religion.
They contend that right would be violated by the imposition of an
eruv
,
even though it would not touch their property. They further assert that
instruments of the State such as the City have the obligation to remain neutral
in religious matters, and that the City cannot be shown to be favouring one
religion over another, or imposing a disadvantage on one religion that it does
not impose on another.

20
Finally, the Intervenant
argues that the Petitioners' complaint is misdirected. It contends that to the
extent they are seeking the type of accommodation Canadian courts have
recognized, they should direct themselves to the Orthodox Jewish religious
authorities instead of the City of Outremont, inasmuch as the City is not the
source of their problem.

III Analysis and Discussion

21
It is worth noting that
Gomery, J. issued what amounted to an interim injunction in this case on April
6. He concluded that “the erection of an
eruv
constitutes a
religious custom or practice having as its objective the fuller participation
of orthodox Jews in the celebration of religious holidays”, and that
“the denial ... of the right to erect an
eruv
or its removal by
the municipal authorities would
prima facie
constitute a violation of
their fundamental freedom of conscience and religion”. He thus ordered
the City “not to interfere with or take down
eruvs
erected by the
Petitioners during the period of April 7 to April 15, 2001”, that is,
during Passover.

22
There is not the
slightest evidence in the record that the implementation of the Order of
Gomery, J. was the source of any inconvenience, let alone hardship, to
Outremont residents who are not Orthodox Jews. Indeed, when she was examined on
discovery on May 17 this year, Mme Fortin did not point to any inconvenience
caused by the Order of Gomery, J. The only physical limitation she identified
when she was examined on her affidavit was that the presence of an
eruv

on the apartment building in which she lives would prevent her from flying a
kite. In response to a direct question, however, she declined to say whether
she has ever tried to fly a kite in front of her residence or whether she ever
otherwise engages in flying kites.

23
Apart from Outremont,
the Court has not been informed of any other municipality anywhere in Canada or
elsewhere in the world that has acted in a similar manner to prevent the
installation of
eruvin
. How or why Outremont has managed to achieve such
isolation, especially from sister municipalities on the Island of Montreal,
remains a mystery, but it is not a subject on which the Court intends to
speculate.

24
The concept of religious
freedom in Canada is well anchored in the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

and the
Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
. It is also
acknowledged that prior to the enactment of the Charters, courts in this
country were rendering judgments in which the principles of freedom of religion
were applied.
2
Although no law or regulation is
being attacked in these proceedings, the case law decided under the Charters is
useful to ascertain the limits of the rights themselves and the corresponding
obligations of regulatory authorities. Without purporting to be exhaustive, the
case law shows that:

Charter
rights, including freedom
of religion, must be given a generous and purposive interpretation without
however going beyond the actual purpose of the right in question;
3

The right of freedom of religion
includes the right to practice the religion and to openly demonstrate or
manifest that practice, while all the while insuring that no injury is caused
to one's neighbours or their right to hold and display different beliefs;
4

In determining what essential
practices are in any religion, the role that the practices and beliefs play in
the religion must be analyzed;
5

Where there is a conflict between
the exercise of a
Charter
right and some perceived public interest or private
concern, reasonable accommodation, meaning accommodation up to the point of
undue hardship, must be shown to facilitate the exercise of the
Charter
right;
6

Laws or regulations that purport
to limit the exercise of
Charter
rights on public property, such as on public
utility poles and at airport concourses, must be interpreted in such a manner
as to facilitate the
Charter
right if the proposed use of the
Charter
right is
not unreasonable;
7

In certain circumstances, freedom
of religion cannot be invoked successfully to avoid compliance with laws of
general application.
8

25
In this case, the City
of Outremont is not being asked to expend public funds, to advance the precepts
of Orthodox Judaism, or to associate itself or its citizens in any way with the
erection of
eruvin
. It is being asked to tolerate the barely visible
wires or lines traversing City streets, and not to take them down when they are
erected. In doing so, it is not being asked to associates itself with the
Orthodox Jewish faith any more or less than it is associates itself with
Christianity when it allows Christmas decorations to be displayed on City
property, including City Hall, or when it tolerates the ringing of church bells
on Sunday morning to summon Christians to worship.

26
The American case of
Smith
v. Community Board No. 14 et al.

9
makes
the point clearly. There, an issue arose as to the propriety of a municipal
regulatory authority having authorized the construction and maintenance of an
eruv

in Queens County. Mr. Smith applied to restrain the defendant from further
construction, maintenance and use of an
eruv
in light of the
establishment clause of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution,
which provides that “Congress shall make no law respecting the
establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof”.

27
In dismissing the
application for an injunction, Goldstein, J. found that the U.S. Constitution
mandated accommodation of religious practices, and that the impugned actions
before him “did not establish religion but were a valid accommodation to
religious practice”.

28
Canada does not have a
provision in its Constitution that is identical to the one that was analyzed by
Goldstein, J. in the
Smith
case.

29
That being said, the
concept of accommodation to the exercise of guaranteed freedoms, including
freedom of religion, is very much a part of the constitutional fabric in this
country, as Prof. Woehrling points out in his learned study of the subject-
L'accommodation
raisonnable et l'adaptation de la société à la
diversité religieuse
.
10
When instruments of the State are
called upon to implement a measure of accommodation of a religious practice,
there is at a minimum the potential for conflict between the duty to
accommodate and the obligation of neutrality. Prof. Woehrling cites American
authors who describe this phenomenon as one of “natural
antagonism”.
11
Indeed, the natural antagonism to
which he refers is very much in evidence in this case.

30
The first issue to be
determined is whether the Petitioners' freedom of religion includes the rights
they are claiming here, and if so, whether they are entitled to accommodation
from the City of Outremont to the extent that the use of air space over City
streets is involved.

31
At the outset, the
Intervenant contends that in considering this question, the Court should
decline to exercise its discretion in favour of the Petitioners because of
their delay in seeking declaratory redress from the Superior Court.
12

Mr. Rosenberg, for example, states in one of the letters he sent the Mayor that
he has been a resident of Outremont for over forty years, yet the matter is
only being raised now.

32
In this respect, as the
Court has already noted, it is not clear from the material in the record
precisely how long
eruvin
have been put up in Outremont. The conduct of
the municipality in dismantling them, however, is of recent origin, and there
is no doubt that the City has only recently taken the firm position that it
will not tolerate their erection. The Petitioners moved with considerable
dispatch to initiate these proceedings once the City had turned down their
formal request for accommodation in October last year, and accordingly they are
not precluded by reason of a supposed acquiescence over many years from seeking
the relief they claim.

33
On the substantive
issue, the Court is satisfied that the materials in the record, and in
particular those produced with the affidavit of Rabbi Merling, demonstrate that
the concept of an
eruv
is firmly established in the precepts of the
Orthodox Jewish faith. In particular,
eruvin
facilitate the
participation of all members of the community in attendance at worship and in
subsequent gatherings that are related to the observance of the Sabbath.

34
For example, when
leaving his or her home on the Sabbath, an Orthodox Jew would not be able to
lock the door to the house because he or she could not take a set of keys once
he or she stepped outside the house. The inevitable consequence of the
prohibition is that someone would have to remain at home and thus miss the
Sabbath services. The alternative would be to leave the house unlocked, which
is not a particularly palatable option for obvious reasons. Having an
eruv

in place allows such a person to have all of the family members in the home
enjoy the benefits of worship. In this regard, the Court endorses the comments
of Gomery, J. in this case that are set out in paragraph [21] above.

35
In light of the
foregoing, the Court considers that the circumstances revealed by the evidence
are distinguishable from those canvassed by Rochon, J. in
Syndicat
Northcrest v. Amselem et al.

13
In that case, he held that in order
for it to be considered that the freedom of religion of an Orthodox Jew was
violated because a provision in a declaration of co-ownership effectively
prevented him from building a
succoth
, it would have to be shown that
the provision, directly or indirectly, required him to act in a way that was
contrary to his religion, or to refrain from doing something that was
considered mandatory by his religion. With the assistance of conflicting expert
evidence, and after analyzing the conduct of the applicants before him, Rochon,
J. found that the practice was optional, and therefore, that there was no
violation of their freedom of religion.

36
In this case, the Court
finds, based on the record before it and the representations of counsel, that
the erection of an
eruv
is essential for the attendance of Orthodox Jews
at Sabbath services, and their participation in related activities upon the
completion of the services. Doing so does not “overshoot” the
purpose of the guarantee, to use the expression of Dickson, J. (as he then was)
in
Big M Drug Mart
, but rather fulfills the purpose of the guarantee and
provides the Petitioners with “the full benefit of the
Charter
's
protection”.
14
The fact that an
eruv
also
facilitates the accomplishment of other activities that may be entirely
secular, such as walking a baby in a stroller, is entirely beside the point,
and is not relevant to its main purpose and the application of the
Charter

guarantee.

37
It is of course true
that the restrictions that an
eruv
is meant to alleviate are not imposed
by the City of Outremont but rather by Orthodox Judaism. That does not make the
understandable desire of the Petitioners to erect
eruvin
to be any less
a matter of their religious beliefs that they are entitled to have recognized
as such.

38
As far as accommodation
is concerned, it is apparent that an
eruv
is already an accommodation
that is available to Orthodox Jews to deal with the prohibition of moving
things from one domain to another. The suggestion that the Petitioners should
therefore address their concerns to Orthodox Jewish religious authorities
instead of the City of Outremont is unmeritorious.

39
Neither counsel opposing
the application suggested, by evidence or otherwise, to whom such a request
should be addressed, how its outcome might be determined, or whether such an
application was even available to be entertained. On the assumption for
purposes of discussion that such an recourse to religious authorities exists,
it is easy to imagine that the Petitioners would have some difficulty
explaining why they should be granted a religious exemption that does not
appear to be necessary for other members of the Orthodox Jewish faith in
neighbouring communities on the Island of Montreal.

40
The Court therefore
rejects this ground of defence.

41
The City argued its
contention that it has an obligation as a matter of law to remain strictly
neutral and not to show favour to one religion over another most forcefully.

42
The provisions in the
Charters would certainly prevent any instrument of the State from establishing
an official religion or discriminating against a particular religion. That
being said, the provisions of Canadian and Quebec law are not entirely free
from reference to religion or certain aspects of religion. As will be seen
below, Quebec law takes specific account of Christian religious holidays and
provides certain financial benefits for all religious institutions. It
therefore cannot be said that the Quebec legislature strictly applies the
concept of absolute neutrality in matters of religion.

43
The preamble to the
Canadian
Charter
, for example, states that “Canada is founded on principles
that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law”. In Quebec,
Article 6 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
makes Sunday, Good Friday,
Easter Monday, and Christmas Day (referred to neutrally as December 25)
non-juridical days. In addition, paragraph 12 of section 204 of the
Municipal
Taxation Act
15
exempts immovables belonging to a
religious institution from the payment of municipal or school real estate
taxes.

44
In any event, as
previously mentioned in paragraph [25], the accommodation the Petitioners seek
does not purport to require the City of Outremont to endorse or in any way to be
associated with Orthodox Judaism, but only to tolerate a religious practice
that has not been shown to cause any inconvenience or undue hardship to
Outremont residents. To the extent that some residents in the affected area
contend that the granting of the Petitioners' claim will involuntarily place
them in some kind of religious zone from which they cannot escape as long as
they live there, counsel for the Petitioners' is right to point out that the
area within an
eruv
is only a religious zone for those who believe it to
be one. That belief is limited to the practitioners of Orthodox Judaism, and
not to residents who do not belong to that faith.

45
The City also expressed
its concern about the use of the air over City streets that are part of the
public domain. It is concerned about the potential for claims of a similar
nature relating to other parts of the public domain that might be asserted if
the Court finds that the Petitioners should prevail.

46
There is no doubt that
the City has an interest in regulating the use of the public domain, including
the air over City streets. In this instance, however, the City declined to
exercise its regulatory authority because of the position it took that Quebec
law mandated absolute religious neutrality and thus prevented it from acceding
to the Petitioners request for accommodation. The Court holds and emphasizes
that it considers the City's position in this regard to be wrong as a matter of
law. On the contrary, the City has a constitutional duty to provide accommodation
for religious practices that do not impose undue hardship on its residents.
16

47
The City can quite
properly regulate the erection of
eruvin
in a manner that facilitates
the exercise of the right while all the while prescribing the means by which
the right is exercised. This would undoubtedly include matters such as the
height of the structures and the number of
eruvin
that might be erected
on each street within the affected area. It remains an option for the City to
exercise such regulatory control.

48
Finally, although the
Court is mindful of the City's concerns about the effect of the Petitioner's
claim being granted in terms of the precedent it might create for the use of
the public domain by others invoking freedom of religion or other
Charter

rights, counsel for the City did not buttress his submission by reference to
any consequential havoc that has occurred in other municipalities on the Island
of Montreal where the erection of
eruvin
has been permitted. The Court
might have expected there to be evidence in that regard if indeed
eruvin

have created additional and unexpected burdens in Montreal, Town of Mount
Royal, Ville St. Laurent, Dollard-des-Ormeaux and Côte St. Luc. The
absence of any such evidence is sufficient to dispose of this
“floodgates” argument, which is often an unsuccessful one of last
resort in
Charter
cases.

49
The Court will therefore
issue a declaration in favour of the Petitioners.

50
Next, the Court must
consider the form of the relief to be granted. As a matter of law, it is not
disputed that in declaratory proceedings, if the Court concludes that an
applicant is entitled to a declaration, the Court is free to frame the
declaration in an appropriate manner.
17

51
In this case, the
declarations mentioned in paragraph [3] are indeed somewhat vague, and the
Court is concerned with their enforceability as framed. They also purport to
benefit parties who are not before the Court. In addition, they go beyond what
is necessary for immediate purposes by proposing the kinds of limits that the
Petitioners would be prepared to accept.

52
While recognizing the
Petitioners' right to erect
eruvin
where the owners of buildings
consent, the Court considers that it would be preferable to allow the City of
Outremont to regulate details such as their height above ground, the number of
eruvin

to be permitted per block, and what needs to be done when new ones are created
or existing ones are removed. The City is in a much better position than this
Court to make such determinations, and it will undoubtedly want to do so
without delay. Nevertheless, the immediate exercise by the Petitioners of the
rights declared by this judgment is not subject to being delayed while the City
ponders what to do. Rather, it is up to the City to adopt a regulatory scheme
that facilitates the exercise of the rights as promptly as it judges advisable.

53
Finally, the
Petitioners' contend that provisional execution should be granted. Apart from
several specific circumstances mentioned in Article 547 of the
Code of Civil
Procedure
, the penultimate paragraph gives the Court discretion to order
provisional execution notwithstanding appeal “for any other reason deemed
sufficient, in particular where the fact of bringing the case to appeal is
likely to cause serious or irreparable injury, for the whole or part only of a
judgment”. This particular provision of Art. 547
C.C.P.
has been
interpreted as giving courts a considerable degree of discretion, but that the
party seeking to obtain provisional execution must establish the special reason
that amounts to a proper exception to the general rule that an appeal that is
regularly brought suspends the execution of the judgment against which it is
taken.
18

54
There was
no proof of any inconvenience or undue hardship caused by the presence of
eruvin

elsewhere on the Island of Montreal, and nothing untoward in Outrement was
revealed to the Court arising out of the interim Order of Gomery, J. The Court
therefore considers that the continuing infringement of the Petitioners' rights
based on freedom of religion, in the absence of any demonstrable harm,
constitutes a sufficient reason to make this judgment executory notwithstanding
appeal. An order to that effect will issue accordingly.

IV Disposition

55
The Court
maintains the Petitioners' motion for declaratory judgment in part, dismisses
the contestation of the Respondent City of Outremont and the intervention of
the
Mouvement Laïque Québécois
, with costs in both
cases, and declares that:

A) The Petitioners
are entitled to establish
eruvin
linking buildings above ground by the
attachment of a string or similar device along with associated rods, with the
consent of the owners of such buildings, the whole within the area of the City
of Outremont described on the map attached to the affidavit of Michael
Rosenberg dated June 7, 2001, that is, the area bounded to the west by Stuart
Avenue, to the north by Van Horne Avenue, to the east by Hutchison Avenue, to
the south by St. Joseph Boulevard, and to the southeast by Côte St.
Catherine Road;

B) The Respondent
City of Outremont may not dismantle such
eruvin
once erected, but may in
the future regulate their usage in a manner that facilitates the exercise of
the Petitioners' rights as specified herein.

further orders the present judgment to be executory notwithstanding appeal.
